chapter_title: Concerning the Four Things over which People kill

spiritual_reading.full_translation:
The first murderous ruling love is the craving to gratify the outer self, by which a person makes bodily delight the end, so that the understanding is dulled and the inward life falls into forgetfulness of higher things.

The second is the profanation of conjunction, when what ought to be a chaste union of good and truth is turned into unbridled and promiscuous mingling, so that the affection of union is defiled and mutual relation is reduced to appetite.

The third is the love of possession for its own sake, when a person gathers what has no use and calls it blessedness, taking pride in what is merely accumulated while removing it from any service to life.

The fourth is the love of dominion, from which come contentions, condemnations, and hostile judgments stirred up against one another; and when one will overcomes another, rule becomes tyranny, and renown in outward life is received as a reward.

All who attach themselves to these four universal ends—celebrated in common speech and common desire in the merely worldly mind—strain to bring them into effect among themselves and to multiply them in their societies.

But the Divine enters as judgment, setting discernment between opposites, and making an actual separation of living good and truth from deadening evil and falsity.

Therefore such corrupt ends do not remain joined to what is eternal; they are cast off, and the life that made them ruling comes to its end.

paragraph_translations.translation: The first murderous ruling love is the craving to gratify the outer self, by which a person makes bodily delight the end, so that the understanding is dulled and the inward life falls into forgetfulness of higher things.
paragraph_translations.connection: BEGINS the list of ruling corruptions that destroy spiritual life.
paragraph_translations.notes: The phrasing about making thought heavy and the soul forgetful required compression into dulled understanding and forgetful inward life.

paragraph_translations.translation: The second is the profanation of conjunction, when what ought to be a chaste union of good and truth is turned into unbridled and promiscuous mingling, so that the affection of union is defiled and mutual relation is reduced to appetite.
paragraph_translations.connection: DEVELOPS the theme by moving from bodily indulgence to profaned union.
paragraph_translations.notes: The repeated and tangled wording about various forms of fornication required synthesis into a single spiritual act: promiscuous conjunction.

paragraph_translations.translation: The third is the love of possession for its own sake, when a person gathers what has no use and calls it blessedness, taking pride in what is merely accumulated while removing it from any service to life.
paragraph_translations.connection: CONTINUES by shifting from profaned affection to the worship of externals.
paragraph_translations.notes: “Useless riches” translated as possessions without use; the core is pride in means divorced from ends.

paragraph_translations.translation: The fourth is the love of dominion, from which come contentions, condemnations, and hostile judgments stirred up against one another; and when one will overcomes another, rule becomes tyranny, and renown in outward life is received as a reward.
paragraph_translations.connection: DEVELOPS into social evils that arise when self-rule becomes the end.
paragraph_translations.notes: “Trials” and “accusations” taken as condemnatory judgment; “name in the world” rendered as renown in outward life.

paragraph_translations.translation: All who attach themselves to these four universal ends—celebrated in common speech and common desire in the merely worldly mind—strain to bring them into effect among themselves and to multiply them in their societies.
paragraph_translations.connection: SUMMARIZES the communal propagation of the four ruling loves.
paragraph_translations.notes: “On every tongue” and “praised” compressed into celebrated in common speech and desire; “assemblies” rendered as societies.

paragraph_translations.translation: But the Divine enters as judgment, setting discernment between opposites, and making an actual separation of living good and truth from deadening evil and falsity.
paragraph_translations.connection: SHIFTS from human striving to Divine discrimination and separation.
paragraph_translations.notes: “Judge of the worlds” translated as the Divine acting as judgment; light/darkness expanded into good-truth versus evil-falsity.

paragraph_translations.translation: Therefore such corrupt ends do not remain joined to what is eternal; they are cast off, and the life that made them ruling comes to its end.
paragraph_translations.connection: CONCLUDES with the inevitable severing and spiritual death of these loves.
paragraph_translations.notes: “Leave them behind and die” treated as separation from eternal life, culminating in the end of that life-state.

spiritual_reading.overall_coherence: Coherent as a single spiritual warning: four ruling loves destroy spiritual life, are propagated socially, then are judged and separated by the Divine; the voice is consistent, with only minor strain where the second paragraph’s wording is repetitive and required consolidation.

findings.diagnosis: Clean correspondential teaching: a vice is explained by its spiritual effect (thickening thought, producing forgetfulness). No narrative break; this is the substrate voice setting up a functional chain (indulgence → mental heaviness → oblivion).
findings.evidence: Text: “the desire of people; in that they would eat… so that their thought is made heavy and their soul becomes forgetful.” The spiritual reading did not stumble here; it simply “compressed” the causal phrasing. The spiritual sense arises from what the act does (makes thought heavy, makes soul forgetful), not from any jurisdictional or named administration.

findings.diagnosis: Genuine difficulty from damaged/duplicated wording, not a foreign voice. The paragraph is semantically consistent with the list, but the surface text shows copying/jogging errors (repetition, broken syntax), which forced the spiritual reader to synthesize. This is not an administrative insertion; it is a corrupt/garbled line within the same moral-causal register.
findings.evidence: Text is visibly tangled: “fornication [and adultery] fornication [with men] men and women [with women] in it with each other.” The spiritual reading explicitly notes it “required synthesis” because of “repeated and tangled wording.” That stumble is best explained as textual corruption (dittography and fragmentary restoration brackets), not a shift to governance-teaching (no ranks, stations, named powers, or jurisdictions appear).

findings.diagnosis: Clean correspondential teaching: wealth is condemned specifically as ‘useless’ (non-functional), and pride is shown as the inner motion. The passage stays inside the fourfold vice-catalogue and continues the same causal-moral voice.
findings.evidence: Text: “wealth; and [the gathering of possessions] the useless riches in [which] they shall pride themselves without [use].” The spiritual reading’s key move—“possessions without use”—is directly generated by the text’s own functional criterion (“without use”), confirming substrate correspondential method (value determined by use).

findings.diagnosis: Clean correspondential teaching with social extension: ‘war’ is unpacked by its operations (disputes, accusations, trials, victory/tyranny, seeking a ‘name’). No named administrators; the logic is functional (what war produces in communal life).
findings.evidence: Text: “war; and the disputes, the [accusations] and the trials… Someone is victor… in tyranny, so that they have received a name in the world.” The spiritual reading did not report a narrative break; it naturally derived “dominion/tyranny” and “renown,” i.e., spiritual meanings arise from described effects rather than from who governs what.

findings.diagnosis: Clean summarizing line that binds the four items into a universal/social propagation statement. Still correspondential: the emphasis is on human attachment and generative effort (“struggle so that they might generate them”), not on cosmic offices or jurisdictions.
findings.evidence: Text: “All people… who side with these four major things… on every tongue… and are praised… they struggle so that they might generate them [in their assemblies].” The spiritual reading’s paraphrase (“celebrated… strain to bring them into effect… multiply… societies”) matches the text’s own verbs (“side with,” “praised,” “struggle,” “generate”), with no noted stumble or foreign terminology.

findings.diagnosis: Potential seam marker, but not an administrative overlay. The ‘Judge of the worlds’ could be a later doctrinal titling, yet the sentence’s function is still correspondential: judgment is defined by separation (light/darkness; good/wicked). It continues the narrative rather than interrupting it.
findings.evidence: Text: “[But the Judge of the worlds comes between them,] he separates the Light from the Darkness, the good from the wicked;” The bracketed opening clause reads like a slightly more titled/theological header, while the operative teaching is functional (“separates”). The spiritual reading notes only a “shift” in action (human striving → divine discrimination) but no incoherence; the story flows directly into separation and outcome.

findings.diagnosis: Clean conclusion: eschatological/moral outcome stated plainly (impermanence of the four loves; abandonment; death). This closes the chapter’s narrative without adding new taxonomies or administrative inventories.
findings.evidence: Text: “they will not remain… for eternity; rather they shall leave them behind and die.” The spiritual reading treats this as the inevitable severing and end-state; no stumble is reported and the logic follows immediately from ¶7’s separation.

textual_criticism.summary: No administrative overlay blocks or clear insertions. The chapter is overwhelmingly correspondential and narratively coherent as a fourfold vice-catalogue followed by judgment/separation and mortality. One localized textual problem occurs in ¶3 (dittography/garbling in the sexual-misconduct list), best treated as damaged text rather than an insertion. ¶7 contains slightly heightened titular language (“Judge of the worlds”) that could reflect minor doctrinal framing, but it does not disrupt the functional narrative and does not warrant excision or annotation.

harmonized_paragraphs.text: The first thing is [the desire] of people; in that they would eat [for the increase] of their body [so that their thought is made heavy and their soul becomes forgetful]
The second is [sexual inter]course; [the defilement of the body] fornication [and adultery] fornication [with men] men and women [with women] in it with each other.
The third thing is wealth; and [the gathering of possessions] the useless riches in [which] they shall pride themselves without [use] from it.

The fourth is war; and the disputes, the [accusations] and the trials that they instigate against each other. Someone is victor over another, with each other in tyranny, so that they have received a name in the world.
All people, they who side with these four major things that [a]re on every tongue [in the] world [and are praised] they struggle so that they might generate them [in their assemblies] among them.
[But the Judge of the worlds comes between them,] he separates the Light from the Darkness, the good from the wicked;
For they will not remain with them for ete[rni]ty; rather they shall leave them behind and die.

changes_summary: No changes were made. All critic recommendations were “none” (Findings 1–7), with ¶3 noted as damaged but not an insertion and therefore not subject to excision.
